the concept of "missing mass" emerged from experimental attempts to measure the masses of hypernuclei. During the 1960s, Lee and Yang suggested that this same missing mass might actually correspond to a new form of nuclear binding, which they termed "beta mass." They proposed that if beta mass existed, it would enable endothermic beta decays with negative $Q$-values among hypernuclei. This idea was later explored by Dalco, Gal, and Grimes, who investigated the implications for the ratio of anti-up to anti-down baryon number densities in the universe and concluded that hypernuclei would not support the existence of beta matter. Most recently, endothermic beta decays have been observed in a specific isotopic chain of ordinary nuclei, sparking renewed interest in the possibility of endothermic decays within hypernuclei. This review outlines the current understanding of these decays, detailing how recent theoretical work has evaluated the feasibility of endothermic alpha, beta, and combined alpha-beta decays in hypernuclei. Additionally, it summarizes the potential astrophysical and cosmological consequences of hypernuclei and distinguishes between the concepts of beta mass and binding energy, clarifying common misconceptions in the literature regarding the definition of beta mass and its relationship to chemical ionization. Finally, the review outlines open questions and suggests directions for future research. These endothermic decays are also relevant to the study of ultra-high-energy cosmic ray air showers, where they could influence hadron-nucleus inelastic cross sections and the production of strange baryons in atmospheric interactions; consequently, dedicated measurements of such endothermic decays in laboratory environments are recommended to refine cosmic ray hadron-nucleus interaction models.
